newsitem.title: UKRAINE: US defence secretary at NATO exercise in Ukraine.
newsitem.headline: US defence secretary at NATO exercise in Ukraine.

text.p: Entertained with folk dancing and American jazz, U.S. Defence Secretary William Cohen on Friday visited the first NATO military peacekeeping exercise held in this sprawling former Soviet republic.

He praised Ukraine for hosting the 1,100 troops from 13 western and other former Communist states, including 106 U.S. soldiers, at the wind-up of a week-long exercise called "Cooperative Neighbour". It was the first NATO "Partnership for Peace" (PFP) exercise staged in Ukraine.

Standing beside host Defence Minister Olexander Kuzmuk, Cohen called the operation "the embodiment of Europe's new security architecture and of Ukraine's key role as a cornerstone in that architecture."

The troops jointly practised rescue and protection of civilians, as well as providing a buffer zone between two mythical warring states. In addition to Ukraine and the United States, soldiers from Bulgaria, the Czech Republic, Georgia, Germany, Greece, Italy, Macedonia, Moldova, the Netherlands, Romania, and Slovakia participated.

At a colourful closing ceremony, Cohen was entertained at the Trans-Carpathian Training District parade field by a Ukrainian military band playing jazzy American tunes such as "Puttin' on the Ritz" and also saw folk dancers from Greece.

Cohen, on a tour to boost ties with East European states, later flew to Ukraine's capital, Kiev, where he will hold talks on Saturday with President Leonid Kuchma and other senior officials on bilateral military cooperation.

Ukraine is now the third largest recipient of U.S. foreign aid behind Israel and Egypt and the visit came only two days after Kuchma and NATO leaders signed a new partnership charter at a western alliance summit meeting in Madrid.
The agreement will allow the former Soviet republic the right to call for consultations with NATO if it feels threatened from abroad.

The United States has praised Ukraine for getting rid of all of its former Soviet nuclear warheads last year and two months ago agreed to provide an additional $47 million to the Kiev government to help Ukraine destroy long-range missiles on which the warheads were mounted.

Cohen told reporters travelling with him in an interview on his aircraft that the United States was anxious to let Ukraine know that it was still a very important country after it shipped all of its former Soviet nuclear warheads back to Russia last year.
"It made the decision to give up its nuclear weapons at a time when there were questions raised as to whether or not it would still be respected as a country," he said.
"We (the United States) will try to help them modernise their forces in the future and to build this PFP programme."
The agreement signed with Ukraine this week put the sprawling Central European country nearly on a par with Russia in its relations with its former foes in the West.

NATO signed a fuller Founding Act on a new, cooperative relationship with Russia in May. The Ukraine charter is seen as essential to balance the alliance's ties with Moscow, which still has tensions with Kiev over the status of Crimea.

Former U.S. Defence Secretary William Perry, Cohen's predecessor, made a number of visits to Ukraine, whose rich soil has given it a reputation as Central Europe's breadbasket, including the first such major multi-national peacekeeping exercise in a former Soviet state at Lviv last year.
Including the $47 milion promised in May, the United States has pledged to give $345.6 million to Ukraine under a nuclear weapons destruction programme.
